$t=\mathrm{cb}_{U_0}(|x|,g(|x|))$ such that $U_0$ has halted on $x$ by time $t$ with output the
single bit $\mathbf{1}_L(x)$, has visited at most $g(|x|)$ cells by time $t$, and the windowed run
of $U_0$ on $x$ at radius $g(|x|)$ for $t+1$ rounds, starting from the initial configuration with
output-summary tag $0$, stops with exit ``halted'', the configuration of $U_0$ at time $t$, and the
output-summary code of the word consisting of the bit $\mathbf{1}_L(x)$. (The windowed run steps
the machine while its next step stays within cells $[-s,s]$, stops ``halted'' at a halted

the given number of rounds; the summary code is $0$ for empty output, $1$ for the output $[1]$ and

be a binary word and put $k=K_I+K_R+k_G+2$; fix arbitrary contents $\tau_j$ and head positions
$h_j$ of $k$ work tapes over the record alphabet and an output $o$. Let $R$ be the machine that runs
$G$ (bits read as digit symbols) on the tapes $K_I+K_R+2,\dots,k-1$, copies its output onto tape
$1$ and, when $G$ halts, enters a live return state; start it from the initial configuration of $G$
on $x$ placed on those tapes, with the other tapes and heads given by $\tau,h$, tape $1$ empty and
prior output $o$. Then there is $t$ such that: $R$ is in its return state at time $t$ and not
earlier; at time $t$ tape $1$ holds the digits of $\beta_x$ from cell $0$ with its head at
$|\beta_x|$; every tape other than $1$ and the selected ones keeps content $\tau_j$ and head $h_j$;
the output is $o$ at all times up to $t$; at most $k\,(c\,g(|x|)+|\beta_x|+1)$ cells are visited by
time $t$; and at every time up to $t$ each head position $p_j$ satisfies
$|p_j|\le|h_j|+c\,g(|x|)+|\beta_x|$.
\end{lemma}

Let $K,L,t\in\mathbb{N}$, let $R$ be a relation on natural numbers, and let
$\mathrm{Init}$ be a predicate on natural numbers. A natural number $u<K$ satisfies
$\mathrm{Init}(u)$ and is related to $t$ by a walk of length at most $L$ using $R$.

\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.ball}

Let $K,L\in\mathbb{N}$, let $R$ be a relation on natural numbers, and let
$\mathrm{Init}$ and $\mathrm{Acc}$ be predicates on natural numbers. The ball at level
$L$ is the finite set of natural numbers $t<K$ for which there is some $u<K$ satisfying
$\mathrm{Init}(u)$ and connected to $t$ by a walk of length at most $L$ using $R$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Bound along a bounded walk]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.walkLe_lt}

Let $R$ be a binary relation on the natural numbers and let $K,j,c,t$ be natural
numbers. If $c<K$ and there is an $R$-walk from $c$ to $t$ of length at most $j$ whose
vertices are bounded by $K$, then $t<K$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Vertex bound for reachable states]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.Mem.lt}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.Mem.lt}

Let $n$ be a natural number, let $E$ be a relation on the natural numbers, and let

length at most $K$, with every step following $E$ through an intermediate vertex below
$n$. If $t$ belongs to this set for the specified $K,E,L$ and initial predicate, then
$t<K$.

\begin{lemma}[Membership in the reachable set]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.mem_ball}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.mem_ball}

Let $K,L,t$ be natural numbers, let $R$ be a binary relation on the natural numbers, and

vertex reached by a step required to be less than $K$. Then $t$ belongs to the set of
vertices reachable in at most $L$ steps from some $I$-vertex $u<K$ if and only if such a

\begin{lemma}[Monotonicity of reachable sets]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.ball_mono}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.ball_mono}

Let $K$ be a natural number, let $R$ be a binary relation on the natural numbers, and
let $\text{Init}$ be a predicate on the natural numbers. For each natural number $L$, let
the reachable set consist of those numbers below $K$ that can be reached in at most $L$
steps from some number below $K$ satisfying $\text{Init}$, where each step follows $R$ to
a number below $K$. If $L \le L'$, then the reachable set for $L$ is contained in the

\begin{lemma}[Reachability after one additional step]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.mem_succ_iff}

\begin{lemma}[Nonmembership after one additional step]

let $I$ be a predicate on the natural numbers, and suppose $v<K$. The vertex $v$ is not

let $\text{Init}$ be a predicate on the natural numbers. If $u_0<K$ and $\text{Init}(u)$

\begin{definition}[Recursive branching process]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.GS}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.GS}

Let $A,B,\mathrm{Kont}$ be predicates on natural numbers. For zero rounds, the process
at position $t$ and count $c$ holds exactly when $\mathrm{Kont}(c)$ holds. For $r+1$
rounds, it holds when either $A(t)$ holds and the process continues for $r$ rounds at
position $t+1$ with count $c+1$, or $B(t)$ holds and it continues at position $t+1$ with
count $c$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Conjunction at the terminal condition]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.gs_and}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.gs_and}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.GS}

Let $A$, $B$, and $\text{Kont}$ be predicates on the natural numbers, let $Q$ be a
proposition, and let $r,t,c$ be natural numbers. The recursive condition that makes $r$
choices between $A$ and $B$, ending with the condition $\text{Kont}(c')\land Q$, holds at
$(r,t,c)$ if and only if the same recursive condition ending with $\text{Kont}(c')$ holds
there and $Q$ holds.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Finite-set characterization of the recursive condition]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.gs_iff}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.gs_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.GS}
\difficulty{6}
Let $A$, $B$, and $\text{Kont}$ be predicates on the natural numbers, and let $r,t,c$ be
natural numbers. The recursive condition that makes $r$ successive choices between $A$
and $B$, incrementing the counter exactly when $A$ is chosen and ending with
$\text{Kont}$, holds at $(r,t,c)$ if and only if there is a finite set
$T\subseteq\{t,t+1,\ldots,t+r-1\}$ such that $A(y)$ holds for every $y\in T$, $B(y)$
holds for every other $y$ in that interval, and $\text{Kont}(c+|T|)$ holds.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Inner-stage condition on the reachable set]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.gs_inner}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.gs_inner}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.GS, Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.Mem, Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.Mem.lt, Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.ball, Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.gs_iff, Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.mem_ball}
\difficulty{4}
Let $K$ be a natural number, let $R$ be a binary relation on the natural numbers, and
let $\text{Init}$ be a predicate on the natural numbers. For natural numbers $L$ and $v$,

holds—requiring at each selected position $u$ that $u$ is reachable within $L$ steps

condition to hold everywhere; and ending when the counter equals the cardinality of the
reachable set—if and only if every element $u$ of that reachable set satisfies $u\ne v$
and not $R(u,v)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Outer-stage condition on the reachable set]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.gs_outer}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.gs_outer}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.GS, Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.Mem, Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.Mem.lt, Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.ball, Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.gs_iff, Complexity.LogProg.ISCount.mem_ball}
\difficulty{5}
Let $K$ and $L$ be natural numbers, let $R$ be a binary relation on the natural numbers,
and let $\text{Init}$ and $\text{Acc}$ be predicates on the natural numbers. Suppose

\section{Space Complexity --- Logspace --- Path Walk}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.Complexity.SpaceComplexity.Logspace.PathWalk
\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Logspace --- Path Walk: Introduction}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{TCSlib.Complexity.SpaceComplexity.Logspace.PathWalk}.

\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Logspace --- Path Walk: Results}

\begin{definition}[Walk relation of bounded length]
\lean{Complexity.WalkLe}
\statementsource{Vad12}{pdf-bf2ce5422088-p036-b001}
\label{Complexity.WalkLe}
\leanok
Let $E$ be a relation on natural numbers and let $n$ be a natural number. Define
$\operatorname{WalkLe}(j,c,t)$ recursively: for $j=0$, it means $c=t$; for $j+1$, it
means either $c=t$, or there is a natural number $v<n$ such that $E(c,v)$ and
$\operatorname{WalkLe}(j,v,t)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Reflexive bounded walks]
\lean{Complexity.walkLe_refl}
\label{Complexity.walkLe_refl}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.WalkLe}
\difficulty{3}
For every relation $E$ on $\mathbb{N}$ and all $n,j,c\in\mathbb{N}$, there is a walk
from $c$ to itself of length at most $j$, where a walk of length at most zero means
equality and a walk at a positive bound means either equality or an initial step to some
$v<n$ following $E$, followed by a walk with bound one less.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Monotonicity of bounded walks]
\lean{Complexity.walkLe_succ}
\label{Complexity.walkLe_succ}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.WalkLe}
\difficulty{4}
Let $E$ be a relation on the natural numbers and let $n$ be a natural number. If $c$
reaches $t$ by a walk of length at most $j$ that uses only vertices less than $n$ (with
a walk of length zero meaning $c=t$), then $c$ reaches $t$ by a walk of length at most
$j+1$ under the same vertex restriction.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Monotonicity of bounded walks]
\lean{Complexity.walkLe_mono}
\label{Complexity.walkLe_mono}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.WalkLe, Complexity.walkLe_succ}
\difficulty{4}
Let $E$ be a binary relation on the natural numbers and let $n,j,k,c,t\in\mathbb{N}$. If
$j\le k$ and there is a walk from $c$ to $t$ of length at most $j$, with every
intermediate vertex less than $n$ and each step related by $E$, then there is such a
walk of length at most $k$. A walk of length at most $j$ here means equality when $j=0$,
and for a positive bound either equality or an initial step to some $v<n$ with $E(c,v)$
followed by a walk of length at most $j-1$ from $v$ to $t$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Bounded walks give restricted reachability]
\lean{Complexity.walkLe_reach}
\label{Complexity.walkLe_reach}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.WalkLe}
\difficulty{4}
Let $E$ be a relation on the natural numbers, and let $n,j,c,t\in\mathbb{N}$ with $c<n$.
If there is a walk from $c$ to $t$ of length at most $j$, in which each initial vertex
of a step is less than $n$ and each step follows $E$, then $t$ is reachable from $c$ by
a finite sequence of steps whose endpoints are both less than $n$ and whose steps follow
$E$. A walk of length at most $j$ is defined recursively: at bound zero it means $c=t$,
and at a positive bound it means either $c=t$ or there is $v<n$ with $E(c,v)$ and a walk
of length at most $j-1$ from $v$ to $t$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Finite bound for a reflexive transitive walk]
\lean{Complexity.exists_walkLe}
\label{Complexity.exists_walkLe}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.WalkLe}
\difficulty{4}
Let $E$ be a binary relation on the natural numbers and let $n\in\mathbb{N}$. If $t$ is
reachable from $c$ by a finite sequence of steps, each from some $u<n$ to some $v<n$
with $E(u,v)$, then there is a natural number $j$ such that $t$ can be reached from $c$
using at most $j$ steps of this form.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Shortening the walk bound]
\lean{Complexity.walkLe_short}
\label{Complexity.walkLe_short}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.WalkLe, Complexity.walkLe_mono}
\difficulty{6}
Let $E$ be a relation on the natural numbers and let $n,j,c,t\in\mathbb{N}$, with $c<n$
and $t<n$. If there is a walk from $c$ to $t$ of length at most $j$, then there is one
of length at most $n$. A walk of length at most $j$ is defined recursively: at bound
zero it means equality, and at a positive bound it means either equality or an initial
step to some $v<n$ following $E$, followed by a walk with bound one less.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Reachability by a bounded walk]
\lean{Complexity.reach_iff_walkLe}
\label{Complexity.reach_iff_walkLe}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.WalkLe, Complexity.exists_walkLe, Complexity.walkLe_reach, Complexity.walkLe_short}
\difficulty{4}
Let $E$ be a relation on the natural numbers, let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $c,t<n$.
There is a finite path from $c$ to $t$ using steps of $E$ whose endpoints are both less
than $n$ if and only if there is a walk from $c$ to $t$ of length at most $n$, with
every intermediate vertex less than $n$. A walk of length zero is allowed.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[List Index Bound]
\lean{Complexity.lt_of_getD_true}
\label{Complexity.lt_of_getD_true}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
For a Boolean list $l$ and a natural number $i$, if the value of $l$ at index $i$, using
false as the default when the index is out of range, is true, then $i<|l|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Extensionality for equal-length Boolean lists]
\lean{Complexity.ext_getD'}
\label{Complexity.ext_getD'}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
If two Boolean lists have the same length and their entries agree at every index smaller
than that length (using false as the default value for out-of-range indices), then the
lists are equal.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Doubled word at a position]
\lean{Complexity.DblAt}
\label{Complexity.DblAt}
\leanok
For Boolean words $x,u$ and a natural number $q$, say that $u$ is doubled at position
$q$ in $x$ if, for every $i<|u|$, the entries of $x$ at positions $q+2i$ and $q+2i+1$
both equal the entry of $u$ at position $i$. The entries of $x$ at positions $q+2|u|$
and $q+2|u|+1$ must respectively be false and true; any out-of-range list lookup is
interpreted as false.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Word at a position]
\lean{Complexity.PlainAt}
\label{Complexity.PlainAt}
\leanok
For Boolean words $x,u$ and a natural number $r$, say that $u$ occurs at position $r$ in
$x$ if, for every $i<|u|$, the entry of $x$ at position $r+i$ equals the entry of $u$ at
position $i$, and $|x|=r+|u|$. Any out-of-range list lookup is interpreted as false.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Characterization by the Doubled Pair Encoding]
\lean{Complexity.dblAt_iff}
\label{Complexity.dblAt_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.DblAt, Complexity.ext_getD', Complexity.getD_drop, Complexity.lt_of_getD_true, Complexity.pairEncode_getD, Turing.length_pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
For every pair of binary words $x,u$ and every natural number $q$, the condition that
$x$ has the doubled encoding of $u$ starting at position $q$—each bit of $u$ repeated
twice, followed by $01$—holds if and only if the suffix of $x$ beginning at $q$ is the
concatenation of that doubled encoding and the suffix of $x$ beginning at $q+2|u|+2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Characterization of a plain segment]
\lean{Complexity.plainAt_iff}
\label{Complexity.plainAt_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.PlainAt, Complexity.ext_getD', Complexity.getD_drop}
\difficulty{4}
For Boolean words $x$ and $u$ and a natural number $r$, $x$ agrees with $u$ starting at
position $r$ and has length $r+|u|$ if and only if $r\le |x|$ and deleting the first $r$
entries of $x$ gives $u$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Raw path encoding]
\lean{Complexity.pathRaw}
\statementsource{Sav70}{
  pdf-c8033d2fd705-p012-b002,
  pdf-c8033d2fd705-p012-b004
}
\label{Complexity.pathRaw}
\leanok
\uses{Turing.pairEncode}
For a natural number $n$, a Boolean word $M$, and natural numbers $s,t$, define the raw
path encoding by pairing the length-$n$ all-true word with the result of pairing $M$
with the encoding obtained by pairing the binary digit lists of $s$ and $t$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Raw adjacency relation]
\lean{Complexity.rawEdge}
\statementsource{Sav70}{
  pdf-c8033d2fd705-p012-b002,
  pdf-c8033d2fd705-p012-b003
}
\label{Complexity.rawEdge}
\leanok
For a natural number $n$, a Boolean list $M$, and natural numbers $u,v$, declare $u$
adjacent to $v$ when $u<n$, $v<n$, and the entry of $M$ at index $un+v$ is true (an
out-of-range entry is treated as false).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Raw path language]
\lean{Complexity.pathRawLang}
\statementsource{Vad12}{pdf-bf2ce5422088-p035-b005}
\statementsource{Sav70}{
  pdf-c8033d2fd705-p012-b003,
  pdf-c8033d2fd705-p012-b004,
  pdf-c8033d2fd705-p012-b005
}
\label{Complexity.pathRawLang}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.pathRaw, Complexity.rawEdge}
The language consists of Boolean lists $x$ for which there are natural numbers $n,s,t$
and a Boolean list $M$ of length $n^2$ such that $s,t<n$, $x$ is the path encoding
determined by $n,M,s,t$, and there is a finite sequence of raw-adjacency steps from $s$
to $t$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Characterization of the raw path encoding]
\lean{Complexity.eq_pathRaw_iff}
\label{Complexity.eq_pathRaw_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.DblAt, Complexity.PlainAt, Complexity.dblAt_iff, Complexity.pathRaw, Complexity.plainAt_iff, Turing.length_pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
Let $x$ and $M$ be finite Boolean words and let $n,s,t$ be natural numbers. Then $x$ is
the encoding of the pair consisting of $n$ true bits and the nested pair of $M$ with the
pair of the binary expansions of $s$ and $t$ (using the encoding that doubles each bit
of the first component, appends $01$, and then appends the second component) if and only
if all of the following hold: starting at position $0$, the first $n$ bits are each
doubled and followed by the separator $01$; starting at position $2n+2$, the bits of $M$
are each doubled and followed by $01$; starting at position $2n+2+2|M|+2$, the bits of
the binary expansion of $s$ are each doubled and followed by $01$; and starting at
position $2n+2+2|M|+2+2|	ext{binary expansion of }s|+2$, the binary expansion of $t$
appears verbatim and ends exactly at the end of $x$. In each doubled segment, both
copies of every bit agree with the corresponding bit of that segment's word; positions
beyond the end of $x$ are interpreted as false when checking these conditions.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Row-major index bound]
\lean{Complexity.rowMajor_lt}
\label{Complexity.rowMajor_lt}
\leanok
\difficulty{2}
Let $n,u,v\in\mathbb{N}$ with $u<n$ and $v<n$. Then $un+v<n^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Encoded path edge]
\lean{Complexity.pathEdge}
\label{Complexity.pathEdge}
\leanok
For a Boolean list $x$ and natural numbers $n,u,v$, the encoded path relation holds when
the entry of $x$ at index $2n+2+2(un+v)$ is true, with out-of-range entries treated as
false.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Unary block terminator]
\lean{Complexity.UnaryRest}
\label{Complexity.UnaryRest}
\leanok
For a Boolean list $x$ and natural numbers $k,n$, every $i$ with $k\le i<n$ has true
entries at indices $2i$ and $2i+1$; the entries at indices $2n$ and $2n+1$ are
respectively false and true. Out-of-range entries are treated as false.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Matrix block terminator]
\lean{Complexity.MatRest}
\label{Complexity.MatRest}
\leanok
For a Boolean list $x$ and natural numbers $n,i$, each $j$ with $i\le j<n^2$ has equal
entries at indices $2n+2+2j$ and $2n+2+2j+1$. The entries at indices $2n+2+2n^2$ and
$2n+2+2n^2+1$ are respectively false and true; out-of-range entries are treated as
false.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Path acceptance condition]
\lean{Complexity.PathAcc}
\statementsource{Sav70}{
  pdf-c8033d2fd705-p012-b002,
  pdf-c8033d2fd705-p012-b003,
  pdf-c8033d2fd705-p012-b004,
  pdf-c8033d2fd705-p012-b005
}
\label{Complexity.PathAcc}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.DblAt, Complexity.MatRest, Complexity.PlainAt, Complexity.UnaryRest, Complexity.WalkLe, Complexity.pathEdge}
A Boolean list $x$ satisfies the acceptance condition if there exist natural numbers
$n,s,t$ such that the unary block condition holds with parameters $0,n$, the matrix
block condition holds with parameters $n,0$, $s<n$, and the doubled encoding of the
binary digits of $s$ begins at index $2n+2+2n^2+2$. Also, $t<n$, the plain encoding of
the binary digits of $t$ begins at index $2n+2+2n^2+2+2\ell+2$, where $\ell$ is the
number of binary digits of $s$, and there is a walk from $s$ to $t$ of length at most
$n$ using the encoded path relation on an $n$-by-$n$ vertex set.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Unary doubled prefix characterization]
\lean{Complexity.unaryRest_iff}
\label{Complexity.unaryRest_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.DblAt, Complexity.UnaryRest}
\difficulty{3}
For every binary word $x$ and $n\in\mathbb N$, the following are equivalent: at each
pair of positions $2i,2i+1$ for $0\le i<n$, both bits of $x$ are $1$, and the next pair
is $01$; or the first $n$ bits of the word encoded by those doubled positions are all
$1$, with the separator $01$ immediately afterward. In all indexed-bit statements, a
position beyond the end of $x$ is read as $0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Characterization of the matrix remainder condition]
\lean{Complexity.matRest_iff}
\label{Complexity.matRest_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.DblAt, Complexity.MatRest}
\difficulty{5}
For every Boolean word $x$ and natural number $n$, the following are equivalent. First,
for every $j<n^2$, the two bits of $x$ at positions $2n+2+2j$ and $2n+3+2j$ agree, and
the bits at positions $2n+2+2n^2$ and $2n+3+2n^2$ are respectively $0$ and $1$. Second,
there is a Boolean word $M$ of length $n^2$ such that, for each $i<n^2$, the bits of $x$
at positions $2n+2+2i$ and $2n+3+2i$ both equal the $i$th bit of $M$, and the same final
two positions contain $0$ and $1$, respectively. Out-of-range word positions are
interpreted as $0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Characterization of the path encoding]
\lean{Complexity.pathAcc_iff}
\label{Complexity.pathAcc_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.DblAt, Complexity.PathAcc, Complexity.eq_pathRaw_iff, Complexity.matRest_iff, Complexity.pathEdge, Complexity.pathRawLang, Complexity.reach_iff_walkLe, Complexity.rowMajor_lt, Complexity.unaryRest_iff}
\difficulty{6}
For every bit string $x$, the following are equivalent. First, there are $n\in\mathbb
N$, an $n\times n$ Boolean adjacency matrix $M$, and vertices $s,t<n$ such that $x$
begins with $n$ pairs $11$, followed by $01$; then each matrix bit is represented by an
equal pair of bits, followed by $01$; then the binary expansion of $s$ is represented by
equal pairs followed by $01$, and the binary expansion of $t$ follows verbatim and ends
the string. In addition, there is a walk from $s$ to $t$ using at most $n$ edges of the
graph encoded by $M$. Second, $x$ is of the form consisting of the doubled unary
encoding of $n$, followed by the similarly encoded matrix $M$, then the similarly
encoded binary expansion of $s$, then that of $t$, and $t$ is reachable from $s$ in the
directed graph whose vertices are $0,\ldots,n-1$ and whose edges are the true entries of
$M$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Least significant bit decomposition]
\lean{Complexity.bits_eq_cons}
\label{Complexity.bits_eq_cons}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.bits_half, Complexity.LogProg.bits_head_odd}
\difficulty{4}
For every nonzero natural number $w$, its binary expansion written from least
significant bit to most significant bit begins with the bit indicating whether $w$ is
odd, followed by the binary expansion of $\lfloor w/2\rfloor$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Initial Bit Decomposition of a Doubled Encoding]
\lean{Complexity.dblAt_cons}
\label{Complexity.dblAt_cons}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.DblAt}
\difficulty{5}
For every pair of binary words $x,u$, every natural number $q$, and every bit $b$, the
condition that $x$ has the doubled encoding of $b::u$ starting at position $q$—meaning
each bit of $b::u$ occurs twice at its prescribed positions and is followed by the
delimiter $01$—holds if and only if $x$ has $b$ at positions $q$ and $q+1$ and has the
doubled encoding of $u$ starting at position $q+2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Plain prefix after its first bit]
\lean{Complexity.plainAt_cons}
\label{Complexity.plainAt_cons}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.PlainAt}
\difficulty{4}
For Boolean words $x$ and $u$, a natural number $r$, and a bit $b$, $x$ agrees with the
word $b::u$ starting at position $r$ and has length $r+|b::u|$ if and only if $x_r=b$
and $x$ agrees with $u$ starting at position $r+1$ and has length $(r+1)+|u|$. Here
out-of-range entries are read as false.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Quotient and remainder of a successor]
\lean{Complexity.divmod_succ}
\label{Complexity.divmod_succ}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
Let $n>0$ and $i$ be natural numbers. If the remainder of $i$ upon division by $n$,
increased by one, equals $n$, then the quotient of $i+1$ upon division by $n$ is the
quotient of $i$ plus one, and the new remainder is zero. If the remainder of $i$
increased by one is not $n$, then the quotient is unchanged and the new remainder is the
previous remainder plus one.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Characterization of a quotient equal to the divisor]
\lean{Complexity.div_eq_self_iff}
\label{Complexity.div_eq_self_iff}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For natural numbers $n$ and $i$ with $i\le n^2$, one has $i/n=n$ if and only if $i=n^2$.
\end{lemma}

\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Logspace --- Path Walk: further results}

\begin{lemma}[Walks with no edges]
\lean{Complexity.walkLe_zero_iff}
\label{Complexity.walkLe_zero_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.WalkLe}
\difficulty{1}
Let $E$ be a binary relation on $\mathbb{N}$, let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let
$c,t\in\mathbb{N}$. Then $t$ is reachable from $c$ by a walk of at most $0$ edges of $E$
whose vertices after $c$ all lie below $n$ if and only if $c=t$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[First-edge decomposition of bounded walks]
\lean{Complexity.walkLe_succ_iff_head}
\label{Complexity.walkLe_succ_iff_head}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.WalkLe}
\difficulty{1}
Let $E$ be a binary relation on $\mathbb{N}$, let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let
$j,c,t\in\mathbb{N}$. Call $t$ reachable from $c$ within $j$ edges if there is a walk
from $c$ to $t$ using at most $j$ edges of $E$ whose vertices after $c$ all lie below
$n$. Then $t$ is reachable from $c$ within $j+1$ edges if and only if either $c=t$, or
there is a vertex $v<n$ with $E(c,v)$ such that $t$ is reachable from $v$ within $j$
edges.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Last-edge decomposition of bounded walks]
\lean{Complexity.walkLe_succ_iff}
\label{Complexity.walkLe_succ_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.WalkLe, Complexity.walkLe_refl, Complexity.walkLe_succ, Complexity.walkLe_succ_iff_head, Complexity.walkLe_zero_iff}
\difficulty{5}
Let $E$ be a binary relation on $\mathbb{N}$, let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let
$j,c,t\in\mathbb{N}$. Call $t$ reachable from $c$ within $j$ edges if there is a walk
from $c$ to $t$ using at most $j$ edges of $E$ whose vertices after $c$ all lie below
$n$. Then $t$ is reachable from $c$ within $j+1$ edges if and only if either $t$ is
reachable from $c$ within $j$ edges, or there is a vertex $w$ reachable from $c$ within
$j$ edges such that $E(w,t)$ and $t<n$.
\end{lemma}

\section{Space Complexity --- Machines --- ARM}

\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Machines --- ARM: Introduction}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{TCSlib.Complexity.SpaceComplexity.Machines.ARM}.

\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Machines --- ARM: Results}

\begin{definition}[Logarithmic-program instructions]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.Ins}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.Ins}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Mode}
For natural numbers $m,d$ and a label type $\Lambda$, define instructions for a program
with $m$ registers and $d$ deciders, whose branch targets are labels in $\Lambda$. The
instructions increment a register, decrement it with truncated subtraction, clear it,
halve it, branch on whether it is zero or odd, branch on equality of two distinct
registers, call a decider on a virtual input specified by a mode and register arguments,
or return a Boolean answer and halt. They also include checks that the input has the
required unary and canonical binary encoding, branches testing whether a register's
binary expansion matches a specified input component, and branches on equality with the
first or second binary component of a nested input encoding.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Abstract register machine]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ARM}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.ARM}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Ins}
For natural numbers $m,d$ and a label type $\Lambda$, an abstract register machine is a
function assigning to each program label an instruction for a machine with $m$
registers, $d$ deciders, and labels in $\Lambda$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Plain input suffix]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.plainWord}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.plainWord}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.tRun}
For a finite bit string $x$, let $t$ be the length of its initial run of $1$s. The plain
word of $x$ is the suffix obtained by deleting its first $t+2$ bits.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Decoded pair of input words]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.pairWords}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.pairWords}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.tRun, Turing.pairDecode}
For a finite bit string $x$, let $t$ be the length of its initial run of $1$s. Decode
the suffix of $x$ after its first $t+2$ bits using the aligned pair parser; if parsing
is undefined, assign the pair of empty words.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Recovery of the encoded payload]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.plainWord_pairEncode}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.plainWord_pairEncode}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.dbl_replicate, Complexity.LogProg.plainWord, Complexity.LogProg.tRun_pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode_eq_dbl}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$ and bit string $w$, remove from the pairing of the unary
string of $n$ ones with $w$ the initial run of ones together with the following two
separator bits; the remaining string is exactly $w$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Decoding an encoded pair]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.pairWords_pairEncode}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.pairWords_pairEncode}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.dbl_replicate, Complexity.LogProg.pairWords, Complexity.LogProg.tRun, Complexity.LogProg.tRun_pairEncode, Turing.pairDecode_pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode_eq_dbl}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$ and Boolean words $u,w$, remove the leading run of $1$s and
the next two bits from the encoding of the pair whose first component is $1^n$ and whose
second component is the encoding of $(u,w)$. Decoding the remaining word returns
$(u,w)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Abstract machine configuration]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.AConf}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.AConf}
\leanok
For a natural number $m$ and a type of machine states $\Lambda$, an abstract
configuration consists of an optional state, a vector of $m$ natural-number register
values, and an optional Boolean result.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Abstract machine step]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.astep}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.astep}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AConf, Complexity.LogProg.ARM, Complexity.LogProg.ValidPair, Complexity.LogProg.ValidPlain, Complexity.LogProg.callSegs, Complexity.LogProg.pairWords, Complexity.LogProg.plainWord, Complexity.LogProg.vword}
Let $m,d$ be natural numbers, let $\Lambda$ be a type of states, let $A$ assign an
instruction to each state, let an oracle assign a Boolean answer to each of $d$ deciders
and each finite bit string, and fix an input bit string $x$. One step leaves a halted
configuration unchanged; otherwise it executes the instruction at the current state:
increment, truncated-decrement, clear, or halve the selected register and move to the
indicated state; branch to one of two states according as a register is zero, odd, or
equal to another register; or call the selected oracle on the virtual input determined
by the mode, input, and register arguments, then branch according to its answer. A
return instruction halts with its specified Boolean result. A plain- or pair-validity
instruction continues to its specified state when the input has the corresponding valid
encoding, and otherwise halts with result false. The three input-equality instructions
branch according as the selected register's binary word equals, respectively, the plain
payload, the first decoded pair word, or the second decoded pair word.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Abstract machine run]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.arun}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.arun}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AConf, Complexity.LogProg.ARM, Complexity.LogProg.astep}
Let $m,d$ be natural numbers, let $\Lambda$ be a type of states, let $A$ assign an
instruction to each state, let an oracle assign a Boolean answer to each of $d$ deciders
and each finite bit string, and fix an input bit string $x$. Starting from a
configuration $a$, the configuration after $n$ steps is the result of iterating the
one-step transition exactly $n$ times.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Machine simulation phases]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.Ph}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.Ph}
\leanok
Define the finite set of simulation phases to consist of the following distinct symbols:
start, incB, decL, decE, decB, clrE, h0, hF, hT, eqBy, eqBn, vU1, vS, vW0, vWF, vWT,
vrw1, vrw2, vP1($\ell$) for an optional Boolean $\ell$, vP2($b,\ell$) for a Boolean $b$
and optional Boolean $\ell$, jK2, jC, jRB($b$), jI1($b$), jI2($b$) for a Boolean $b$,
jP1, jP2F, jP2T, jD1, jD2F, and jD2T.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Continue machine action]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.goAct}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.goAct}
\leanok
\uses{Turing.Action}
For a natural number $m$ and a type of states $S$, define the action that continues in
state $s$ by leaving the input head and all $m$ work-tape heads stationary, making no
work-tape writes, emitting no output symbol, and setting the successor state to $s$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Return machine action]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.retAct}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.retAct}
\leanok
\uses{Turing.Action}
For a natural number $m$, a type of states $S$, and a Boolean $b$, define the action
that halts and emits $b$ by leaving the input head and all $m$ work-tape heads
stationary, making no work-tape writes, emitting the Boolean symbol $b$, and having no
successor state.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Second rightward scan action]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.rw2Act}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.rw2Act}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.xAct, Turing.Action}
For a register index $r$ and states $s_0,n_x$, define an action depending on an optional
Boolean. When the Boolean is present, it is the action given by the leftward register
action with successor state $s_0$; when it is absent, it is the action given by the
rightward register action with successor state $n_x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Default inactive action]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.junkAct}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.junkAct}
\leanok
\uses{Turing.Action}
For $m$ work tapes over the Boolean alphabet and state set $S$, define the default
action to leave the input head and every work-tape head stationary, make no writes or
output, and halt.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Instruction transition action]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.insTr}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.insTr}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Ins, Complexity.LogProg.Ph, Complexity.LogProg.backAct, Complexity.LogProg.clrEAct, Complexity.LogProg.cmpAct, Complexity.LogProg.dcmp1Act, Complexity.LogProg.dcmp2Act, Complexity.LogProg.decDAct, Complexity.LogProg.decEAct, Complexity.LogProg.decLAct, Complexity.LogProg.eqBAct, Complexity.LogProg.eqCAct, Complexity.LogProg.goAct, Complexity.LogProg.halfLAct, Complexity.LogProg.incBAct, Complexity.LogProg.incCAct, Complexity.LogProg.junkAct, Complexity.LogProg.pskip1Act, Complexity.LogProg.pskip2Act, Complexity.LogProg.retAct, Complexity.LogProg.rewAct, Complexity.LogProg.rw2Act, Complexity.LogProg.skipAct, Complexity.LogProg.toEndAct, Complexity.LogProg.valP1Act, Complexity.LogProg.valP2Act, Complexity.LogProg.valSAct, Complexity.LogProg.valUAct, Complexity.LogProg.valWAct, Complexity.LogProg.xAct, Turing.Action}
Given an instruction with $m$ registers and $d$ available deciders, a label, a phase, an
optional Boolean input symbol, and the current contents of each register, define the
corresponding one-step action of a machine whose states are pairs of labels and phases.
The action is determined by the instruction and phase, with the specified instruction
transitions and the default inactive action in the remaining cases.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Labelled instruction transition action]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.armTr}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.armTr}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.ARM, Complexity.LogProg.Ph, Complexity.LogProg.insTr, Turing.Action}
Let $A$ assign an instruction to each label in a set $\Lambda$. For a label, phase,
optional Boolean input symbol, and register contents, define the one-step action to be
the instruction transition action for the instruction assigned to that label, with
states given by pairs of labels and phases.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Call specification for an instruction]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.insCall}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.insCall}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.CallSpec, Complexity.LogProg.Ins, Complexity.LogProg.Ph}
Given an instruction with $m$ registers and $d$ available deciders and a phase, define
an optional call specification. It is present precisely when the instruction is a call
and the phase is the start phase; it records the chosen decider, input mode, argument
registers, and the positive and negative successor labels paired with the start phase.
In all other cases there is no call specification.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Labelled call specification]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.armCall}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.armCall}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.ARM, Complexity.LogProg.CallSpec, Complexity.LogProg.Ph, Complexity.LogProg.insCall}
Let $A$ assign an instruction to each label in $\Lambda$. For a label and phase, define
the optional call specification by taking the call specification of the assigned
instruction at that phase.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Turing machine for a labelled program]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.armProg}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.armProg}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.ARM, Complexity.LogProg.Ph, Complexity.LogProg.RProg, Complexity.LogProg.armCall, Complexity.LogProg.armTr}
Let $A$ assign an instruction to each label in $\Lambda$, and choose an initial label.
Define a machine with $m$ work tapes and states consisting of a label paired with a
phase. Its initial state is the chosen label paired with the start phase; its transition
function is the labelled instruction transition action, and its call function is the
labelled call specification.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Initial configuration for a register computation]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.aseam}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.aseam}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Ph, Turing.Cfg, Turing.FinTM.bufferTape}
Given an input string $x$ of Boolean symbols, a label $l$, a natural-number value $v(r)$
for each of $m$ registers, and a Boolean output string, define a machine configuration
with state $(l,\mathrm{start})$, input head at the first position, each register tape
containing the binary expansion of its assigned value, every work-tape head at position
zero, and the specified output string.
\end{definition}

\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Machines --- ARM: further results}

\begin{lemma}[Running zero steps]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.arun_zero}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.arun_zero}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AConf, Complexity.LogProg.ARM, Complexity.LogProg.arun}
\difficulty{1}
Let $A$ be an abstract register machine with $m$ registers, $d$ deciders and label set
$\Lambda$, let $\mathcal{O}$ assign a Boolean answer to each decider index $j<d$ and each
bit string, and let $x$ be an input bit string. For every abstract configuration $a$ (an
optional label, a vector of $m$ register values in $\mathbb{N}$, and an optional Boolean
result), running $A$ with oracle $\mathcal{O}$ on input $x$ from $a$ for $0$ steps
yields $a$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[One step at an increment]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.astep_inc}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.astep_inc}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.astep}
\difficulty{1}
Let $A$ be an abstract register machine with $m$ registers, $d$ deciders and label set
$\Lambda$, let $\mathcal{O}$ be an oracle answering each decider on each bit string, let
$x$ be an input bit string, and let $l\in\Lambda$, register values $v$ and an optional
result $\rho$ be given. If the instruction of $A$ at $l$ increments register $r$ and
continues at $l'$, then one step of $A$ from $(l,v,\rho)$ yields
$(l', v[r\mapsto v(r)+1], \rho)$, where $v[r\mapsto k]$ agrees with $v$ except that
register $r$ holds $k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[One step at a decrement]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.astep_dec}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.astep_dec}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.astep}
\difficulty{1}
Let $A$ be an abstract register machine with $m$ registers, $d$ deciders and label set
$\Lambda$, let $\mathcal{O}$ be an oracle answering each decider on each bit string, let
$x$ be an input bit string, and let $l\in\Lambda$, register values $v$ and an optional
result $\rho$ be given. If the instruction of $A$ at $l$ decrements register $r$ and
continues at $l'$, then one step of $A$ from $(l,v,\rho)$ yields
$(l', v[r\mapsto v(r)\dot{-}1], \rho)$, where $\dot{-}$ is truncated subtraction on
$\mathbb{N}$ and $v[r\mapsto k]$ agrees with $v$ except that register $r$ holds $k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[One step at a clear]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.astep_clr}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.astep_clr}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.astep}
\difficulty{1}
Let $A$ be an abstract register machine with $m$ registers, $d$ deciders and label set
$\Lambda$, let $\mathcal{O}$ be an oracle answering each decider on each bit string, let
$x$ be an input bit string, and let $l\in\Lambda$, register values $v$ and an optional
result $\rho$ be given. If the instruction of $A$ at $l$ clears register $r$ and
continues at $l'$, then one step of $A$ from $(l,v,\rho)$ yields
$(l', v[r\mapsto 0], \rho)$, where $v[r\mapsto 0]$ agrees with $v$ except that register
$r$ holds $0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[One step at a halving]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.astep_half}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.astep_half}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.astep}
\difficulty{1}
Let $A$ be an abstract register machine with $m$ registers, $d$ deciders and label set
$\Lambda$, let $\mathcal{O}$ be an oracle answering each decider on each bit string, let
$x$ be an input bit string, and let $l\in\Lambda$, register values $v$ and an optional
result $\rho$ be given. If the instruction of $A$ at $l$ halves register $r$ and
continues at $l'$, then one step of $A$ from $(l,v,\rho)$ yields
$(l', v[r\mapsto \lfloor v(r)/2\rfloor], \rho)$, where $v[r\mapsto k]$ agrees with $v$
except that register $r$ holds $k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[One step at a zero test]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.astep_jz}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.astep_jz}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.astep}
\difficulty{1}
Let $A$ be an abstract register machine with $m$ registers, $d$ deciders and label set
$\Lambda$, let $\mathcal{O}$ be an oracle answering each decider on each bit string, let
$x$ be an input bit string, and let $l\in\Lambda$, register values $v$ and an optional
result $\rho$ be given. If the instruction of $A$ at $l$ tests register $r$ for zero with
branch targets $l_1$ and $l_0$, then one step of $A$ from $(l,v,\rho)$ yields
$(l_1,v,\rho)$ if $v(r)=0$ and $(l_0,v,\rho)$ otherwise.

\begin{lemma}[One step at a parity test]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.astep_jodd}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.astep_jodd}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.astep}
\difficulty{1}
Let $A$ be an abstract register machine with $m$ registers, $d$ deciders and label set
$\Lambda$, let $\mathcal{O}$ be an oracle answering each decider on each bit string, let
$x$ be an input bit string, and let $l\in\Lambda$, register values $v$ and an optional
result $\rho$ be given. If the instruction of $A$ at $l$ tests register $r$ for oddness
with branch targets $l_1$ and $l_0$, then one step of $A$ from $(l,v,\rho)$ yields
$(l_1,v,\rho)$ if $v(r)\bmod 2=1$ and $(l_0,v,\rho)$ otherwise.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[One step at an equality test]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.astep_jeq}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.astep_jeq}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.astep}
\difficulty{1}
Let $A$ be an abstract register machine with $m$ registers, $d$ deciders and label set
$\Lambda$, let $\mathcal{O}$ be an oracle answering each decider on each bit string, let
$x$ be an input bit string, and let $l\in\Lambda$, register values $v$ and an optional
result $\rho$ be given. If the instruction of $A$ at $l$ compares registers $r$ and $s$

## ===== blueprint/src/chapter/Complexity/SpaceComplexity/Machines/ARMLoops.tex =====

\section{Space Complexity --- Machines --- ARMLoops}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.Complexity.SpaceComplexity.Machines.ARMLoops
\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Machines --- ARMLoops: Introduction}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{TCSlib.Complexity.SpaceComplexity.Machines.ARMLoops}.

\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Machines --- ARMLoops: Results}

\begin{definition}[Bounded admissible configurations]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AConf, Complexity.LogProg.ARM, Complexity.LogProg.PreS}
Given a program with $m$ registers, an input bit string $x$, and a natural number $B$,
call a configuration admissible with bound $B$ if it satisfies the program’s
precondition for $x$ and every register contains a number at most $B$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Register bound guard]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe.of_preS}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe.of_preS}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AConf, Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe, Complexity.LogProg.PreS}
\difficulty{1}
Let $A$ be a register program, $x$ an input, $B$ a natural number, and $a$ a
configuration consisting of a control state, register values, and an optional answer. If
the precondition of $A$ holds at $a$ for input $x$, and every register value is at most
$B$, then $a$ satisfies the guard requiring both conditions.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Reachability under endpoint equality]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.reach_of_eq}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.reach_of_eq}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AConf, Complexity.LogProg.AReach}
\difficulty{1}
Let a deterministic register machine, oracle, input, and configuration property $G$ be
fixed. If configuration $b$ is reachable from configuration $a$ by a finite run whose
configurations before the endpoint satisfy $G$, then any configuration equal to $b$ is
also reachable from $a$ by such a run.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Register Transfer Loop]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.move_run}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.move_run}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AReach, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.refl, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.step, Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe, Complexity.LogProg.PreS, Complexity.LogProg.astep, Complexity.LogProg.reach_of_eq}
\difficulty{5}
Let $A$ be a register program with $m$ registers and $d$ oracle deciders, let $x$ be an
input, and let $B$ be a natural-number bound. Suppose distinct registers $r,t$ and
states $l,l_x,l_1,l_2$ satisfy: at $l$ the program branches to $l_x$ when register $r$
is zero and to $l_1$ otherwise; at $l_1$ it decrements $r$ and proceeds to $l_2$; and at
$l_2$ it increments $t$ and returns to $l$. For every $k$ and register assignment $v$
with $v(r)=k$, with every register value at most $B$, and with $v(t)+v(r)\le B$, the
configuration at $l$ reaches the configuration at $l_x$ with $r$ set to zero and $t$ set
to its original value $v(t)+v(r)$, all other registers unchanged, and no answer
recorded; every configuration before the final one satisfies the program's precondition
and has all register values at most $B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded run for a register transfer]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.move2_run}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.move2_run}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AReach, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.refl, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.step, Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe, Complexity.LogProg.PreS, Complexity.LogProg.astep, Complexity.LogProg.reach_of_eq, Complexity.LogProg.register_update_le}
\difficulty{5}
Let $A$ be a register program, let an oracle and input word be fixed, and let $B$ be a
natural-number bound. Suppose distinct registers $r,t,t'$ and states $l,l_x,l_1,l_2,l_3$
satisfy: at $l$ the program branches on whether register $r$ is zero, sending the zero
case to $l_x$ and the other case to $l_1$; at $l_1$ it decrements $r$ and continues to
$l_2$; at $l_2$ it increments $t$ and continues to $l_3$; and at $l_3$ it increments
$t'$ and returns to $l$. For every natural number $k$ and register valuation $v$ with
$v(r)=k$, all register values at most $B$, and $v(t)+v(r)\le B$ and $v(t')+v(r)\le B$,
there is a finite run from $(l,v,\mathrm{none})$ to $(l_x,v',\mathrm{none})$ in which
$r$ is set to $0$, while $t$ and $t'$ are each increased by the initial value $v(r)$ and
every other register retains its value. At every configuration before the final one, the
active instruction satisfies its applicable side condition (register comparisons use
distinct registers, input comparisons use valid encodings, and call arguments are
distinct), and every register value is at most $B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded register transfer run]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.dmove_run}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.dmove_run}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AReach, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.refl, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.step, Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe, Complexity.LogProg.PreS, Complexity.LogProg.astep, Complexity.LogProg.reach_of_eq, Complexity.LogProg.register_update_le}
\difficulty{5}
Let $A$ be a register program, fix an oracle and input, and suppose registers $r$ and
$t$ are distinct. Suppose the instructions at states $l,l_1,l_2,l_3$ are, respectively,
a zero test on $r$ branching to $l_x$ or $l_1$, a decrement of $r$ leading to $l_2$, an
increment of $t$ leading to $l_3$, and an increment of $t$ leading back to $l$. For
every $k$ and register valuation $v$ with $v(r)=k$, all registers bounded above by $B$,
and $v(t)+2v(r)\le B$, there is a finite run from state $l$ with valuation $v$ to state
$l_x$ with $r$ reset to zero and $t$ increased by $2v(r)$, leaving the other registers
unchanged; every configuration before the endpoint satisfies the guard that its
precondition holds and all registers are at most $B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Register Subroutine Run]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.sub_run}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.sub_run}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AReach, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.refl, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.step, Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe, Complexity.LogProg.PreS, Complexity.LogProg.astep, Complexity.LogProg.reach_of_eq, Complexity.LogProg.register_update_le}
\difficulty{5}
Let $A$ be a register program, let $q,r$ be distinct registers, and suppose its
instructions at states $l,l_1,l_2$ are respectively: branch to $l_x$ when register $q$
is zero (with the other branch to $l_1$), decrement $q$ and go to $l_2$, then decrement
$r$ and return to $l$. For every $k\in\mathbb N$ and register valuation $v$ with
$v(q)=k$ and every register value at most $B$, there is a finite run from state $l$ to
state $l_x$ that satisfies the guard requiring the program's side conditions and every
register value to be at most $B$ at each earlier step. The final valuation sets $q$ to
$0$, decreases $r$ by $k$ using truncated subtraction, and leaves all other registers
unchanged; the final result is unset.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Repeated halving after a countdown]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.halve_run}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.halve_run}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AReach, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.refl, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.step, Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe, Complexity.LogProg.PreS, Complexity.LogProg.astep, Complexity.LogProg.reach_of_eq, Complexity.LogProg.register_update_le}
\difficulty{6}
Let $A$ be a register program, let $l,l_x,l_1,l_2$ be labels, and let $c,r$ be distinct
registers. Suppose label $l$ tests whether register $c$ is zero, its positive branch
decrements $c$ and goes to $l_2$, and $l_2$ halves register $r$ and returns to $l$. For
every $k\in\mathbb N$ and register assignment $v$ with $v(c)=k$ and $v(s)\le B$ for
every register $s$, the program can reach the configuration at $l_x$ obtained by setting
$c$ to zero and replacing $r$ by $v(r)/2^{v(c)}$, with no result bit, while every
configuration before the final one satisfies the guard requiring the program's
precondition and all registers to be at most $B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded run of a register copy routine]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.copy_run}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.copy_run}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AReach, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.trans, Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe, Complexity.LogProg.move2_run, Complexity.LogProg.move_run, Complexity.LogProg.reach_of_eq, Complexity.LogProg.register_update_le}
\difficulty{4}
Let $A$ be a register program with oracle and let $B$ be a natural number. Choose
distinct registers $src,dst,z$ and states $l,l_1,l_2,l_3,l_4,l_5,l_6,l_x$. Suppose the
program instructions at these states implement the following routine: at $l$, branch on
whether $src=0$; if nonzero, decrement $src$, increment $dst$, and increment $z$, then
return to $l$; if zero, branch on whether $z=0$; while $z$ is nonzero, decrement $z$,
increment $src$, and repeat that branch; when $z=0$, proceed to $l_x$. For every initial
register assignment $v$ with $v(z)=0$, all register values at most $B$, and
$v(dst)+v(src)\le B$, there is a finite run from state $l$ to state $l_x$ that changes
only $dst$, setting it to $v(dst)+v(src)$, and leaves every register value at most $B$.
Every configuration before the final one satisfies the program's guard: any
equality-branch registers are distinct, any input-dependent checks are valid on $x$, and
any call uses an argument list without repetitions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Register doubling by a logarithmic loop]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.shl_run}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.shl_run}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AReach, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.refl, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.step, Complexity.LogProg.AReach.trans, Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe, Complexity.LogProg.PreS, Complexity.LogProg.astep, Complexity.LogProg.dmove_run, Complexity.LogProg.move_run, Complexity.LogProg.reach_of_eq, Complexity.LogProg.register_update_le}
\difficulty{6}
Let $A$ be an instruction program on $m$ registers, with configurations consisting of a
control state, register values in $\mathbb{N}$, and an optional Boolean result; let an oracle
assign a Boolean answer to each of $d$ deciders on Boolean-string inputs. Suppose the
transitions from states $l,l_1,\ldots,l_8$ are respectively: test whether register $c$
is zero (branching to $l_x$ if so and $l_1$ otherwise); decrement $c$ and go to $l_2$;
test whether $r$ is zero (branching to $l_6$ if so and $l_3$ otherwise); decrement $r$
and go to $l_4$; increment $z$ and go to $l_5$; increment $z$ and return to $l_2$; test
whether $z$ is zero (branching to $l$ if so and $l_7$ otherwise); decrement $z$ and go
to $l_8$; and increment $r$ and return to $l_6$. Assume $c,r,z$ are pairwise distinct
registers. For every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and register assignment $v$ with $v(c)=k$, $v(z)=0$,
every register value at most $B$, and $v(r)2^{v(c)}\le B$, this program reaches the
configuration with state $l_x$, register $c$ set to zero, register $r$ set to
$v(r)2^{v(c)}$, all other registers unchanged, and no result. Every configuration
strictly before that endpoint satisfies the guard: it meets the instruction-specific
safety condition and all register values are at most $B$.
\end{theorem}

\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Machines --- ARMLoops: further results}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded halting run of an embedded block]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.AHalt.embed_guardLe}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.AHalt.embed_guardLe}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AHalt, Complexity.LogProg.AHalt.embed, Complexity.LogProg.ARM, Complexity.LogProg.AReach, Complexity.LogProg.GuardLe, Complexity.LogProg.Ins.embed, Complexity.LogProg.RegExt, Complexity.LogProg.preS_embed}
\difficulty{4}
Let $A$ be an abstract register machine with $m$ registers, $d$ deciders and label set
$\Lambda$, none of whose instructions is an input-format check, and let $D$ be a
register machine with $m'$ registers, $d'$ deciders and label set $\Lambda'$. Let
$\rho:\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\to\{0,\ldots,m'-1\}$ be injective, let $\sigma$ map deciders of $A$
to deciders of $D$, let $\iota:\Lambda\to\Lambda'$, let $k$ assign an exit label of $D$
to each Boolean, and let $r_0$ be a register of $D$; suppose that for every label $l$ of
$A$, the instruction of $D$ at $\iota(l)$ is the instruction of $A$ at $l$ with registers
renamed along $\rho$, deciders along $\sigma$, labels along $\iota$, and each answer $b$
replaced by a jump to $k(b)$ (a zero test of $r_0$). Fix an oracle for the deciders of
$D$, an input $x$, bounds $B\le B'$, and a register assignment $e$ of $D$ with every
value at most $B'$. Suppose that $A$, querying decider $j$ through decider $\sigma(j)$ of
the oracle, halts with answer $b$ from label $l$ with registers $v$ and no answer, every
configuration before halting meeting the syntactic instruction preconditions and having
all registers at most $B$. Then for every register assignment $v'$ of $D$ with
$v'(\rho(r))=v(r)$ for all $r$ and $v'(r')=e(r')$ for every $r'$ outside the range of
$\rho$, there is a register assignment $v_2'$ such that $v_2'$ agrees with $e$ outside the
range of $\rho$, $v_2'(\rho(r))\le B$ for every register $r$ of $A$, and $D$ has a finite
run from label $\iota(l)$ with registers $v'$ and no answer to label $k(b)$ with registers
$v_2'$ and no answer, every configuration before the end meeting the syntactic
instruction preconditions of $D$ on $x$ and having all registers at most $B'$.
\end{theorem}

## ===== blueprint/src/chapter/Complexity/SpaceComplexity/Machines/ARMProof.tex =====

\section{Space Complexity --- Machines --- ARMProof}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.Complexity.SpaceComplexity.Machines.ARMProof
\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Machines --- ARMProof: Introduction}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{TCSlib.Complexity.SpaceComplexity.Machines.ARMProof}.

\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Machines --- ARMProof: Results}

\begin{definition}[Reachability under an invariant]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.AReach}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.AReach}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AConf, Complexity.LogProg.ARM, Complexity.LogProg.arun}
Let $A$ be a program, let an oracle assign a Boolean answer to each decider and bit
string, let $x$ be an input, and let $G$ be a predicate on configurations. A
configuration $a'$ is reachable from $a$ in some finite number $T$ of steps if the run
from $a$ on $x$ reaches $a'$ at time $T$ and every configuration at a time $t<T$
satisfies $G$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Halting with a specified answer]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.AHalt}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.AHalt}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AConf, Complexity.LogProg.ARM, Complexity.LogProg.arun}
Let $A$ be a program, let an oracle assign a Boolean answer to each decider and bit
string, let $x$ be an input, and let $G$ be a predicate on configurations. The run from
configuration $a$ halts with answer $b$ if, for some natural-number time $T$, its state
component is empty and its output component is $b$ at time $T$, and every configuration
at a time $t<T$ satisfies $G$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Additivity of abstract run lengths]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.arun_add}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.arun_add}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AConf, Complexity.LogProg.arun}
\difficulty{3}
For any register program $A$, oracle function $o$, input $x$, initial configuration $a$,
and natural numbers $s,t$, running $A$ for $s+t$ steps from $a$ gives the same
configuration as running it first for $s$ steps and then for $t$ more steps.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Reflexivity of guarded reachability]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.AReach.refl}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.AReach.refl}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AConf, Complexity.LogProg.AReach}
\difficulty{2}
For any natural numbers $m,d$, type $\Lambda$, register program $A : \Lambda \to
\mathrm{Ins}(m,d,\Lambda)$, oracle $O : \mathrm{Fin}(d) \to \{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}$,
input bit string $x$, predicate $G$ on configurations, and configuration $a$, there is a
time $T$ such that the run from $a$ is at $a$ after $T$ steps and $G$ holds at every
configuration at each time $t<T$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Transitivity of Constrained Reachability]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.AReach.trans}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.AReach.trans}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.AConf, Complexity.LogProg.AReach, Complexity.LogProg.arun_add}
\difficulty{5}
Fix a program, oracle, input, and predicate $G$ on configurations. If there is a finite
run from $a$ to $b$ and a finite run from $b$ to $c$, with every configuration before
each run's endpoint satisfying $G$, then there is a finite run from $a$ to $c$ with
every configuration before its endpoint satisfying $G$.
\end{lemma}

Let $A$ be a program with $m$ registers, and let $x$ be an input bit string. A
configuration satisfies the precondition when, if its control state is an instruction
comparing two registers, those registers are distinct; if it compares a register with
the input payload, the input has the prescribed valid plain encoding; if it compares a
register with either component of a paired payload, the input has the prescribed valid
paired encoding; and if it is a decider call, the list of argument registers has no
repetitions. All other configurations satisfy the precondition.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Logspace decidability by an oracle register program]

natural number $K$, such that for every input $x$, the run starting at $\ell_0$ with all

\begin{definition}[Instruction relabeled into a larger machine]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.Ins.embed}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.Ins.embed}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Ins}
Let $\rho$ map the $m$ registers of a register machine into $m'$ registers, $\sigma$ map its
$d$ oracle deciders into $d'$ deciders, $\iota$ map its labels $\Lambda$ into labels
$\Lambda'$, let $\kappa:\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}\to\Lambda'$ assign an exit label to
each answer, and let $r_0$ be one of the $m'$ registers. The embedding of an instruction
renames every register it mentions by $\rho$ (elementwise on a call's argument list), its
decider by $\sigma$ and every target label by $\iota$, keeping the kind of instruction, except
that the instruction ``halt with answer $b$'' becomes a zero test of $r_0$ whose two branches
both jump to $\kappa(b)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Register extension along a register map]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.RegExt}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.RegExt}
\leanok
Let $\rho$ map $m$ registers into $m'$ registers, let $e$, $v'$ assign naturals to the $m'$
registers and $v$ to the $m$ registers. Then $v'$ extends $v$ along $\rho$ with background $e$
when $v'(\rho(r))=v(r)$ for every register $r$, and $v'(r')=e(r')$ for every register $r'$ not
in the range of $\rho$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Register writes preserve extensions]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.RegExt.update}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.RegExt.update}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.RegExt}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\rho$ be an injective map from $m$ registers into $m'$ registers, let $e,v'$ assign
naturals to the $m'$ registers and $v$ to the $m$ registers, and suppose $v'$ extends $v$ along
$\rho$ with background $e$ (that is, $v'(\rho(r))=v(r)$ for all $r$ and $v'$ agrees with $e$
off the range of $\rho$). Then for every register $r$ and every $n\in\mathbb N$, the assignment
$v'$ with $\rho(r)$ set to $n$ extends $v$ with $r$ set to $n$, along $\rho$ with background
$e$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Syntactic preconditions from the instruction]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.preS_of_ins}

Suppose that if the instruction at $\ell$ is an equality test of registers $r,s$ then
$r\ne s$; if it is an oracle call then its argument registers are pairwise distinct; if it
compares a register with the payload of a plain input then $x$ has the form
$\langle 1^n,w\rangle$ with $w$ not ending in $0$; and if it compares a register with
either payload of a pair input then $x$ has the form $\langle 1^n,\langle u,w\rangle\rangle$
with neither $u$ nor $w$ ending in $0$. Then the configuration $(\ell,v,a)$ satisfies the syntactic
step preconditions of $A$ on $x$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Preconditions carry over to an embedded block]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.preS_embed}

answer and $r_0$ a register of $D$, and suppose that for every label $\ell$ the instruction of

every register assignment $v'$ of $D$ the live configuration of $D$ at $\iota(\ell)$ with
registers $v'$ satisfies $D$'s syntactic step preconditions on $x$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[One step of an embedded block]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.astep_embed}

answer and $r_0$ a register of $D$, such that for every label $\ell$ the instruction of $D$ at

\end{lemma}

position, register-tape contents and head positions, simulated work-tape contents and

the call specification at node $l$ is $cs$. Starting from the compiled machine in its
second return phase at $l$, with segment index $s$, direction bit $dir$, result bit $b$,
arbitrary register and decider tapes, head positions, and output, take an input-head
position $ip$ whose value is $j$, where $j\le |x|$. Through every time $t\le j+1$, all
work-tape head positions remain unchanged; after $j+1$ steps the configuration has
input-head position $1$, the same tapes, work-head positions and output, and state given
by the return successor determined by $cs,l,s,dir,b$ and register index $0$.
\end{lemma}

to the return successor for argument position $a+1$, with register $rr$'s head at zero

head either remains at its initial position or, for register $rr$, lies between $-1$ and
the maximum of its initial position and $0$; the decider tape head positions remain

\begin{definition}[Register position on the left side]

register index in $\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$, and let $\mathrm{dir}$ be a Boolean. Define the
left-side indicator to be true exactly when $s<a+1$, or when $s=a+1$ and $\mathrm{dir}$
is false.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Restored register position]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.retPos}

\leanok

Let a call specification have an ordered list of register indices, and let $rp_0$ assign
an integer position to each register. For a natural number $a$, define the restored
position of register $r$ to be $0$ if $r$ occurs in that list at an index less than $a$;
otherwise define it to be its position $rp_0(r)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Register position constraints]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.RegBox}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.RegBox}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.CallSpec}
Let a call specification list register indices, let $c_0$ assign an integer position to
every register, and let $W$ assign a finite Boolean word to every register. A position

when $r$ is absent from the call's list; when $r$ occurs in the list, it lies between
$-1$ and the length of $W(r)$, inclusive.
\end{definition}

decider tapes, decider-head positions, and output, and with each argument register head
reset according to the return-position rule for the full argument list.

\section{Space Complexity --- Machines --- Clean Sweep}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.Complexity.SpaceComplexity.Machines.CleanSweep
\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Machines --- Clean Sweep: Introduction}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{TCSlib.Complexity.SpaceComplexity.Machines.CleanSweep}.

\subsection*{Space Complexity --- Machines --- Clean Sweep: Results}

\begin{definition}[Cleaning phases]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.CPh}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.CPh}
\leanok
The four cleaning phases are marking the current cell, moving right over marked cells,
moving left while erasing marked cells, and moving right back to the origin mark while
erasing it.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Cleaning machine states]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.CleanSt}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.CleanSt}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.CPh}
For a state type $S$ and a natural number $k$ of work tapes, the cleaning machine has
states for initialization from each state $q\in S$, simulation from each state $q\in S$,
and cleaning each tape $i<k$ in any of the four cleaning phases.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Idle work-tape action]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.idleK}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.idleK}
\leanok
For a natural number $k$, the idle action on each of the $k$ work tapes is the pair
consisting of no symbol and the sign $0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Cleaning-phase tape action]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.clAct}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.clAct}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.CleanSt, Turing.Action}
For a cleaning tape index $i$ among $k$ tapes, an optional work-tape write instruction
$w_D$, an optional mark-tape write instruction $w_M$, a head movement $m\in\{-1,0,1\}$,
and an optional successor cleaning state $s$, define an action on $2k$ work tapes that
leaves the input head and output unchanged. On tape $i$ in each block of $k$ tapes it
performs the respective write instruction and movement $m$; on every other tape it
leaves the symbol and head position unchanged. Its successor state is $s$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Next cleaning tape]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.clNext}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.clNext}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.CleanSt}
For an index $i$ among $k$ tapes, define the next cleaning state to be the cleaning
state for tape $i+1$ in the marking phase when $i+1<k$, and undefined otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Cleaned machine]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.cleanTM}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.cleanTM}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.CleanSt, Complexity.LogProg.clAct, Complexity.LogProg.clNext, Complexity.LogProg.idleK, Turing.MultiTapeTM}
Given a deterministic Turing machine $M$ with $k$ work tapes, Boolean alphabet, and
state set $S$, and an initial state $q_0\in S$, define a machine with $2k$ work tapes
and cleaning states. It starts in the initialization state for $q_0$, marks the origin
on the added tapes, and then simulates $M$ on the first $k$ tapes while maintaining
marks on the added tapes; when $M$ halts, it proceeds through the cleaning phases to
erase those marks and return the work tapes to blank, halting after the cleaning
process.
\end{definition}

\lean{Complexity.LogProg.ccfg}

\uses{Complexity.LogProg.CleanSt, Turing.Cfg}

two collections of $k$ work-tape contents $D_t,M_t$ and head positions $D_p,M_p$, and an
output string, define the configuration on $2k$ work tapes by concatenating the two
collections of tape contents and the two collections of head positions, in that order.
\end{definition}

\end{lemma}

$a-1$ with head at $a$; all other tapes, the input-head position, and the output are
unchanged.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Boolean segment]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.Seg}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.Seg}
\leanok
A segment is a pair consisting of a finite Boolean word and a Boolean flag.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Rendering a segment]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.render}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.render}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg, Turing.dbl}
For a segment consisting of a Boolean word $w$ and a flag $b$, its rendering is the
bitwise doubling of $w$ when $b$ is true, and is $w$ itself when $b$ is false.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Rendered segment length]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.rlen}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.rlen}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg}
For a segment $(w,b)$, define its rendered length to be $2|w|$ if $b$ is true and $|w|$
otherwise, where $|w|$ is the length of the Boolean word $w$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Length of a doubled segment]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.rlen_true}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.rlen_true}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.rlen}
\difficulty{1}
For every Boolean word $w$, the length assigned to the segment $(w,\mathrm{true})$ is
$2|w|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Length of an undoubled segment]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.rlen_false}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.rlen_false}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.rlen}
\difficulty{1}
For every Boolean word $w$, the length assigned to the segment $(w,\mathrm{false})$ is
$|w|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Length of a rendered segment]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.length_render}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.length_render}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg, Complexity.LogProg.render, Complexity.LogProg.rlen}
\difficulty{3}
For any segment consisting of a bit string $w$ and a flag indicating whether it is
doubled, the length of its rendered bit string equals $2|w|$ when the flag is true and
$|w|$ when it is false.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Encoding a list of segments]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.vword}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.vword}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg, Complexity.LogProg.render}
Define the encoding of a list of segments recursively: the empty list encodes as the
empty word, and a one-segment list encodes as the rendering of that segment. For a list
with at least two segments, encode the first segment, append the separator $01$, and
then encode the remaining list.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Segment-list offset]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.off}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.off}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg, Complexity.LogProg.rlen}
Define the offset of a list of segments at a natural number $i$ recursively: it is $0$
when $i=0$ or when the list is empty; for a nonempty list and positive $i$, it is the
rendered length of the first segment plus $2$ plus the offset of the remaining list at
$i-1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Segment lookup with a default]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.seg}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.seg}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg}
A segment is a pair consisting of a finite Boolean list and a Boolean flag. Given a list
of segments and an index, the selected segment is the entry at that index when it
exists, and otherwise is the pair consisting of the empty list and `false`.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Segment lookup at the list head]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.seg_cons_zero}

Let a segment be a pair consisting of a Boolean list and a Boolean. For any segment $s$
and list of segments $R$, looking up position zero in $s :: R$ returns $s$.

\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg, Complexity.LogProg.seg}
\difficulty{1}
Let a segment be a pair consisting of a Boolean list and a Boolean. For any segment $s$,
list of segments $R$, and natural number $i$, looking up position $i+1$ in the list $s
:: R$ returns the same segment as looking up position $i$ in $R$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Successive segment offsets]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.off_succ}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.off_succ}

Let $segs$ be a finite list of segments and let $i$ satisfy $i+1<|segs|$. The offset at
index $i+1$ equals the offset at index $i$, plus the rendered length of segment $i$,

\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Length of a virtual word]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.length_vword}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.length_vword}
\leanok

\leanok

\begin{definition}[Tape positions]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.TPos}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.TPos}
\leanok
A tape position is either the left boundary, the right boundary, or a cell position
specified by a natural-number cell index and a Boolean marker.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Segment word length]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.wlen}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.wlen}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg, Complexity.LogProg.seg}
For a list of segments and a natural-number index, the word length at that index is the
length of the Boolean list in the segment selected there, using the default segment when
the index is out of range.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Validity of a tape position]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.TPos.Valid}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.TPos.Valid}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg, Complexity.LogProg.TPos, Complexity.LogProg.wlen}
Given a list of segments and a natural-number index, a cell position with cell index $c$
is valid exactly when $c$ is less than the word length at that index. The left and right
boundary positions are always valid.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Cell offset]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.cellOff}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.cellOff}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg, Complexity.LogProg.seg}
Given a list of segments, an index $s$, a cell index $c$, and a Boolean marker $p$, the
cell offset is $2c+p$ when the selected segment's flag is true, and is $c$ when that
flag is false; here a Boolean is identified with $0$ or $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Position index]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.vpos}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.vpos}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg, Complexity.LogProg.TPos, Complexity.LogProg.cellOff, Complexity.LogProg.off, Complexity.LogProg.rlen, Complexity.LogProg.seg}
For a list of segments and an index $s$, assign the left boundary the offset preceding
segment $s$, and assign the right boundary that offset plus one and the selected
segment's encoded length. A cell with index $c$ and marker $p$ is assigned the preceding
offset plus one and its cell offset.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Cell Offset Bound]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.cellOff_lt}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.cellOff_lt}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg, Complexity.LogProg.cellOff, Complexity.LogProg.rlen, Complexity.LogProg.seg, Complexity.LogProg.wlen}
\difficulty{4}
Let a segment be a Boolean word together with a flag, and let a finite list of such
segments be given. For indices $s,c\in\mathbb{N}$ and a Boolean $p$, if $c$ is less than
the word length of the defaulted $s$th segment, then the cell offset for that segment
and position is strictly less than its rendered length.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Tape movement rule]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.tmove}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.tmove}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Seg, Complexity.LogProg.TPos, Complexity.LogProg.seg, Complexity.LogProg.wlen}
Given a list of segments, a segment index $s$, a tape position, and a direction in
$	ext{SignType}$, this rule returns a new segment index and tape position. Direction
zero leaves both unchanged. In the positive direction, at cell $c$ with marker $p$, if
the current segment's flag is true and $p$ is false, the marker becomes true; otherwise
the position advances to cell $c+1$ when that cell lies within the segment, and moves to
the right boundary when it does not. From the right boundary, it moves to the left
boundary of segment $s+1$ if that segment exists, and otherwise stays at the right
boundary; from the left boundary, it moves to cell $0$ with marker false if the segment
is nonempty, and otherwise to the right boundary. In the negative direction, at cell $c$
with marker $p$, if the current segment's flag is true and $p$ is true, the marker
becomes false; otherwise the position moves to cell $c-1$ with marker true when $c>0$,
and to the left boundary when $c=0$. From the right boundary, it moves to the last cell
with marker true if the segment is nonempty, and otherwise to the left boundary; from
the left boundary, it moves to the right boundary of segment $s-1$ when $s>0$, and
otherwise stays at the left boundary.
\end{definition}
